interest: This file provides exceptional insight into the complex economic and ecological entanglements between Allied-occupied Japan and civil-war-era China in 1948–1949. It vividly documents the dilemma faced by SCAP officials who had to balance Japan's critical domestic forest conservation needs and postwar industrial rehabilitation against the desperate fuel requirements of Nationalist North China and the U.S. Western Pacific Naval Command at Tsingtao. The verbatim conference transcript in Enclosure 2 offers a rare, detailed view of frontline negotiations between Chinese commercial/diplomatic representatives and SCAP division heads, illustrating the rigid constraints of post-WWII barter trade, currency shortages, and logistical hurdles like harbor freeze-overs. Finally, the December 1949 telegram captures the pivotal transition toward sourcing lumber from Formosa (Taiwan) via the ECA as mainland China fell to Communist forces.
overview: This file (894.6172, Lumbering and Timber Cutting in Japan, July 1948 – December 1949) documents U.S. and Allied occupation policy regarding the export and import of timber in Japan, focusing on two main episodes. The major portion of the file (July 1948) concerns an urgent appeal by the Kailan Mining Administration (KMA) and the Chinese Mission in Japan to barter high-grade coking coal for 250,000 koku of Japanese mine timbers (pit props) needed to avert a total shutdown of North China's coal mines, which fueled regional railways, power plants, Shanghai industries, and the U.S. Navy at Tsingtao. General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (GHQ SCAP), through its Natural Resources Section and Economic and Scientific Section, recommended rejecting the export due to severe domestic timber deficits, heavy overcutting of Japanese softwood forests, paper pulp shortages, and potential harm to Japanese coal production and mine safety. The file concludes with a December 1949 telegram from Tokyo requesting diplomatic and ECA assistance in Taipei to explore the availability, species, and pricing of construction lumber from Formosa (Taiwan) for export to Japan.

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing SCAP findings and recommendations regarding an urgent proposal to export Japanese mine timbers to China in exchange for Kailan coking coal.
subfiles.summary: Richard M. Herndon briefs John M. Allison on Despatch No. 459 from Tokyo regarding the Kailan Mining Administration's request to barter 100,000 tons of coking coal for 250,000 koku of Japanese pit props. The memorandum outlines KMA's critical coal role for Nationalist North China and Shanghai, warning that a mine shutdown would cause severe military and economic fallout. However, it emphasizes that SCAP's Natural Resources Section and Industry Division recommended against the export due to severe softwood overcutting in Japan, pulpwood requirements, and the risk of reducing domestic coal output and increasing mine fatalities.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from Herndon to Allison on Export of Japanese Mine Timbers to China

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch transmitting SCAP staff studies and recommendations opposing the export of Japanese mine timbers to the Kailan Mining Administration in North China.
subfiles.summary: Political Adviser William J. Sebald reports to the Secretary of State on findings by SCAP staff sections regarding an urgent appeal from the Chinese Mission and KMA representatives to barter coking coal for Japanese mine timbers before Qinhuangdao freezes. Although recognizing the political and military importance of KMA coal to Nationalist China and the U.S. Navy at Tsingtao, Sebald explains that Japan faces an acute timber deficit where softwood production exceeds annual growth by more than two to one. He details SCAP's recommendation to deny the timber export to protect Japanese reconstruction, paper production, and mine safety, noting that any credit from future coal deliveries should instead defray China's existing trade deficit with Japan.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 459 from USPOLAD Tokyo on Export of Japanese Mine Timbers to China

subfiles.about: An appeal from the Chief of the Chinese Mission in Japan transmitting a memorandum from Kailan Mining Administration representatives requesting SCAP approval for a timber-for-coal barter.
subfiles.summary: General Shang Chen writes to Major General P. J. Mueller forwarding a July 2, 1948 memorandum from KMA representatives Y. F. Chen and H. H. Faulkner requesting SCAP authorization to procure 200,000 to 250,000 koku of Japanese mine timber. The enclosed memorandum warns that KMA has only two months of timber left and supplies over 75 percent of China's public utilities and railways as well as the U.S. West Pacific Naval Command at Tsingtao. The representatives explain that obtaining timber from North America or other East Asian sources is prohibitively expensive or politically impossible, offering to barter high-grade coking coal shipped to Japan before the winter freeze closes the port of Qinhuangdao.
subfiles.title: Letter from General Shang Chen to Major General P. J. Mueller Enclosing KMA Memorandum on Timber Barter

subfiles.about: Minutes of a SCAP inter-agency conference with Chinese Mission and Kailan Mining Administration officials discussing the proposed barter of mine props for coking coal.
subfiles.summary: Lt. Col. H. B. Donaldson records the minutes of a July 9, 1948 meeting between SCAP staff sections (Natural Resources, Economic and Scientific, Civil Transportation) and representatives of KMA and the Chinese Mission. KMA representatives Chen and Faulkner explain their urgent need for 250,000 koku of Japanese pit props by November 30 to avert mine shutdowns and severe disruptions across Nationalist North China, offering approximately 100,000 tons of coking coal in return. SCAP officers rigorously question the representatives regarding historical supply sources, coal-to-timber ratios, the impossibility of North American imports, shipping allocations, and potential barters for iron ore or pig iron before concluding the session.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for Record on Conference Regarding Export of Mine Props to China

subfiles.about: A classified telegram from Tokyo requesting U.S. consular and ECA assistance in Taipei to investigate the procurement of Formosan construction lumber for Japan.
subfiles.summary: An incoming telegram from Tokyo forwarded via the State Department requests the American Consul in Taipei to coordinate with Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) representative Plate regarding available lumber supplies in Formosa. It states that Japan is interested in obtaining general construction timber and asks for an investigation into available tree species (identified by Japanese names), quantities, delivery schedules, and estimated prices. The telegram was designated for immediate relay and action by ECA authorities in Taipei.
subfiles.title: Incoming Telegram from Tokyo on Procurement of Formosan Lumber
